articles.title: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Rohit Patel is departing Meta after eight years working on AI evaluations and reinforcement learning, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. His startup, Ndoc, aims to take on Microsoft Office Suite.
articles.full_text:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc , a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.

Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan , AI researcher Andrew Tulloch , and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith .

Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow.

The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.  Ndoc brings three components together in one layout.

The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps.

The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers.

The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.  The design reflects Patel’s background.

During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy.

Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work.

For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents. “Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do?

Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.” In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings.

They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.  Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models.

Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models. “I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.” Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself.

He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.

His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone.

At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.” Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.” Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.

OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta , SpaceXAI , and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools.

And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.

Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.  “Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul.

This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil.

No.

Get a tractor.” There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though.

It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows.

Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.  “My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do.

If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.” Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.  As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list.

It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens.

He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.

For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.  “Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.” Topics AI , Enterprise AI , Exclusive , Meta , meta superintelligence labs , Startups When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
articles.full_text:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public.

Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions .

Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1 , none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table.

That’s highly unusual.

In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed.

The reason is Anthropic’s size.

At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.

While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners.

Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.

Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company.

Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic.

Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.

According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30.

That is Anthropic’s entire debt load.

But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable.

Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.

As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books.

It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026.

The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.

Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1.

But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options.

Amazon can waive the cap.

Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.

But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings.

It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30.

Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds.

Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.

Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.

Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic.

The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times , and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.

While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.

The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

articles.title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: The banking giant reminds customers that "you're responsible for activity" resulting from your AI agents' access.
articles.full_text:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.

In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.” You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email.

Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular .

Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it.

Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.

This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money .

As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.

A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media .

But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you.

Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.” (via Bryan Toporek ) Topics agentic payments , AI , Bank of America , Banking , cybersecurity , Fintech , Security When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.title: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Here's a clear explanation of Anthropic's incredibly complex governance structure.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term.

As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.

Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley.

But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.

First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety.

That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.

Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi.

There is one vacancy on the board.

Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity.

The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors.

The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs.

There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now.

The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.

Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors.

If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.

Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT.

When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.

Here’s what all that looks like: The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict.

We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them.

Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place.

Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.

At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.

The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain.

At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.

If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

articles.title: Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn't want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may […]
articles.full_text:
AI Policy Report Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities.

Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities. by Robert Hart Oct 27, 2026, 4:51 PM UTC Link Share Gift Bloomberg via Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow.

Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes .

Anthropic wants to have it both ways.

With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity.

But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.

Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has cited investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year.

Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure.

A “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before…creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested.

But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.

Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation.

Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities.

Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.

Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors.

Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO.

Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board.

Related Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run.

For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious. “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all.

Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law.

It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.

The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.

Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats.

However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters.

Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote.

This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verg e.

The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as reported by The San Francisco Standard .

All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge . “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.” Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well.

But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.” And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures.

Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns.

Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge ’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.

Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving.

In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders.

Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.

But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.

Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it.

Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told The Verge.

Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.

For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways.

But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust.

Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands.

As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
